questions.question: A ball bearing is released from rest and falls a distance l. The time t is measured for several decreasing values of l. Explain how these measurements give g in m s-2, and sketch the graph the student expects.
questions.answer: Plot l against t^2; the straight line through the origin has gradient 0.5g, so g = 2 x gradient.
steps: The ball is released from rest, so u = 0 and l = ut + 0.5gt^2 gives l = 0.5gt^2.
This is a straight line through the origin when l is plotted against t^2, because the gradient 0.5g is constant.
Measure t for each l, then calculate t^2 for each value.
Plot l (y-axis, m) against t^2 (x-axis, s^2) and draw the best-fit straight line through the origin.
Sketch: a straight line through the origin with positive gradient (a curve would show that the acceleration is not constant).
Gradient = 0.5g, so g = 2 x gradient, in m s-2.

questions.question: A sphere released from rest is photographed at constant time intervals. Image 1 shows the release position. Which of the positions P, Q, R or S is the sphere in Image 3? (A P, B Q, C R, D S)
steps: Released from rest at constant acceleration g, the distance fallen s = 0.5gt^2, so s is proportional to t^2.
Image 2 is at time T, so its distance from Image 1 is one gap (call it d); in the diagram the gap between Image 1 and Image 2 equals the spacing between P, Q, R and S.
Image 3 is at time 2T, so its distance from Image 1 is (2)^2 x d = 4d, which is 3 gaps below Image 2.
Counting gaps down from Image 2: P is 1 gap, Q is 2 gaps, R is 3 gaps, so Image 3 is at R.

questions.question: A short wooden rod is released from rest above a light gate. The student uses v^2 = u^2 + 2as with u = 0 and a graph. State the additional measurements needed.
questions.answer: The distance s from the release point to the light gate, and the length d of the rod (to find v = d/t).
steps: With u = 0, v^2 = 2as, so the distance s fallen from rest to the light gate must be measured.
Measure s from the release point of the rod to the light gate with a metre rule.
The velocity at the gate is found from v = d/t, so the length d of the rod must also be measured with a ruler or calipers.

questions.question: Describe how the velocity of the rod as it passes through the light gate can be determined accurately.
questions.answer: Measure the rod length d, then v = d / t, where t is the time the light gate records for the rod to block the beam; use a short rod and repeat.
steps: The light gate timer records the time t for the rod to block the beam as it passes through.
While blocking the beam the rod moves its own length d, so the distance moved during the timed interval is d.
Use v = d / t; for a short rod this average speed through the gate is close to the speed at the gate.
Measure d accurately with a ruler or micrometer, and repeat the release to obtain a mean value.

questions.question: Describe how the student can determine g using a graphical method, with v^2 = 2as and u = 0.
questions.answer: Plot v^2 (y-axis) against s (x-axis); the straight line through the origin has gradient 2g, so g = gradient / 2.
steps: Since u = 0, v^2 = 2as, so v^2 is directly proportional to s.
For each release position s, calculate v = d/t and then v^2.
Plot v^2 on the y-axis against s on the x-axis and draw the best-fit straight line through the origin.
The gradient is 2g, so g = gradient / 2.

questions.question: A sphere is released from rest to determine g. Which two quantities need the fewest measurements? A displacement and initial velocity; B displacement and time; C final velocity and displacement; D final velocity and time.
steps: The sphere is released from rest, so the initial velocity is zero and needs no measurement.
Using s = ut + 0.5gt^2 with u = 0 gives g = 2s / t^2, so one displacement and one time are enough.
A is wrong because the initial velocity is zero and is not a useful measurement.
C and D need the final velocity, which cannot be measured directly without extra measurements.

questions.question: A student times a ball bearing falling from rest through distance s, for a range of values of s. Which row of the table shows the graph whose gradient is g?
steps: Falling from rest with u = 0: s = 0.5gt^2, which can be rearranged to 2s = gt^2.
So a graph of 2s (y-axis) against t^2 (x-axis) is a straight line through the origin with gradient g.
A (s against 2t^2) has gradient g/4, and s against t^2 would have gradient g/2.
C and D give curves, because s is not proportional to t or 2t (s is proportional to t^2).

questions.question: A laboratory strobe has a shorter flash duration than a strobe app, with the same time between flashes. Explain how the shorter duration affects the uncertainty in the distance fallen measured from the photograph.
questions.answer: A shorter flash gives a sharper image with less blur, so the ball position is read more precisely and the uncertainty in distance is reduced.
steps: A longer flash lets the ball move during the flash, so its image is smeared over a range of positions.
A shorter flash freezes the motion, so the image of the ball is sharper.
The edges of the ball can be located more precisely, so each distance measurement has a smaller uncertainty.

questions.question: Explain why a graph of s against t^2 gives a straight line for a ball falling from rest.
questions.answer: With u = 0 and constant a = g, s = 0.5gt^2, so s is directly proportional to t^2 and the graph is a straight line through the origin.
steps: The ball falls from rest, so u = 0, and its acceleration is constant at g.
The equation s = ut + 0.5at^2 becomes s = 0.5gt^2.
This has the form y = mx with y = s, x = t^2 and gradient m = 0.5g, which is constant.
A constant gradient passing through the origin gives a straight line.

questions.question: Using the student's graph of s against t^2, determine the acceleration of free fall g.
questions.answer: g = 10 m s^-2 (about 9.9 to 10 m s^-2)
steps: From s = 0.5gt^2, the gradient of the s against t^2 graph is 0.5g, so g = 2 x gradient.
Use a large triangle on the best-fit line, which passes through the origin and the point (0.040 s^2, 0.20 m).
g = 2 x 5.0 = 10 m s^-2 (the top point (0.0625, 0.31) gives 4.96 and g = 9.9 m s^-2).

questions.question: A student measures the time t for a ball bearing to fall different distances s from rest and plots a graph with gradient equal to g. Which row of the table shows this graph?
steps: From rest, s = 0.5gt^2, so 2s = gt^2.
Plotting 2s on the y-axis against t^2 on the x-axis gives a straight line through the origin with gradient g.
A (s against t^2) has gradient 0.5g, while C (t^2 against s) has gradient 2/g and D (t^2 against 2s) has gradient 1/g.

questions.question: A ball bearing falls from rest through 50 cm in 0.32 s. Which expression gives its acceleration in m s-2? A 1 divided by 0.32^2; B 0.5 x 0.32; C 100 divided by 0.32^2; D 50 x 0.32. (The operator symbols in the text are partly garbled; A and C are divisions.)
steps: From s = ut + 0.5at^2 with u = 0, a = 2s / t^2.
Convert the distance to metres: 50 cm = 0.50 m.
a = 2 x 0.50 / 0.32^2 = 1 / 0.32^2 = 9.77 m s-2, which matches option A.
C gives 100 / 0.32^2, which would be in cm s-2 when s is in cm, so it is not in m s-2.

questions.question: A steel ball bearing falls a measured distance in air to determine g. Which condition is needed for an accurate value? A air flow is laminar; B time to reach terminal velocity is short; C the ball starts to fall before the timer starts; D air resistance and upthrust are both negligible.
questions.answer: D - air resistance and upthrust are both negligible.
steps: For the acceleration to equal g, the only force acting must be the weight.
Air resistance and upthrust must therefore be negligible.
A is not needed: laminar flow only matters if drag is significant.
B is wrong: reaching terminal velocity quickly means drag is significant, so the acceleration is no longer g.
C is wrong: the timer must start when the ball is released.

questions.question: A student gets g = 11.2 m s-2 by dropping a metal sphere and measuring distance and time. Which could explain the difference from the accepted value? A air resistance not negligible; B measured distance greater than actual distance; C sphere did not fall vertically; D measured time greater than actual time.
questions.answer: B - the measured distance was greater than the actual distance.
steps: From g = 2s / t^2, a larger measured s gives a larger calculated g.
11.2 m s-2 is larger than 9.81 m s-2, so the measured distance is too large or the measured time is too small.
A would reduce the acceleration, giving a smaller g.
D makes t too large, giving a smaller g; C does not make the calculated g too large.

questions.question: A student uses a stopwatch to time a ball bearing falling a measured distance and calculates g greater than 9.81 m s-2. Which could explain this? A ball bearing moving downwards when the stopwatch starts; B ball bearing moving upwards when the stopwatch starts; C stopwatch started before the ball is dropped; D stopwatch stopped after the ball lands.
questions.answer: A - the ball is already moving downwards when the stopwatch starts.
steps: g = 2s / t^2, so a g that is too large means the measured time t is too small.
A: if the ball is already falling when timing starts, the timed interval is shorter than the true fall time, so g is too large.
B: if the ball is moving upwards at the start, the timed interval is longer, so g is too small.
C and D both make the timed interval longer, so g would be too small.

questions.question: An object on the Moon falls 0.32 m from rest in a time of 0.63 s. Which expression gives the acceleration due to gravity on the Moon? Options A to D are not in the extracted text.
steps: Released from rest, u = 0, so s = 0.5gt^2 and g = 2s/t^2.
Substituting s = 0.32 m and t = 0.63 s gives g = (2 x 0.32) / 0.63^2, which is option C.
Numerically g = 0.64 / 0.397 = 1.6 m s^-2, a sensible value for the Moon (about one sixth of 9.81 m s^-2).
A is s/(2t), B is s/(2t^2) = g/4 and D is 2s/t (the final speed), so none of them gives g.

questions.question: A student drops a ball from several heights, measures the time to reach the ground, and plots height on the y-axis to find g using a graph. Which row of the table is correct for the graph?
questions.answer: C: (time)^2 on the x-axis, gradient g/2
steps: Falling from rest, h = 0.5gt^2.
With h on the y-axis and t^2 on the x-axis this is y = (g/2)x, a straight line through the origin with gradient g/2.
Plotting against t (rows A and B) would give a curve, not a straight line, so those cannot have a constant gradient.
D is wrong because the gradient is half of g, not twice g.
